question: Why do free-roaming dog population-management programs sometimes fail to achieve intended public-health outcomes, and which measurement and intervention dependencies are missing?
authority: All model-generated nodes are neutral candidates; no empirical or clinical outcome accepted.

rounds.focus: Whether dog turnover and movement undermine sustained rabies vaccination coverage in sterilization-led free-roaming dog programs, and whether surveillance and human post-exposure prophylaxis access explain differences in reported public-health outcomes.

hypotheses: Births, abandonment and immigration may replenish susceptible dogs, so sterilization and vaccination procedure counts may overstate sustained vaccination coverage.
Programs with similar sterilization intensity may have different rabies outcomes because vaccination continuity, surveillance and timely human post-exposure prophylaxis differ.

A counterargument is that population stabilization may add little short-term rabies-control benefit when sustained dog vaccination is adequate; integrated programs are needed to distinguish these contributions.
Missing repeated population denominators, movement data, vaccination histories and linked exposure-to-treatment records may prevent attribution of apparent program failure.

proposition_sample.statement: The Anuradhapura study evaluated a zoned CNVR program over five years.
Free-roaming dogs were sampled through capture of sexually intact dogs along predefined routes with standardized effort.
Owned dogs entered the Anuradhapura clinic component through voluntary presentation.
The reported number of free-roaming dogs requiring sterilization decreased from 1,368 to 484.
Annual decreases in community dog counts per unit effort were not statistically significant.
The abstract reports statistically significant buffer-intervention findings restricted to particular sex and zone combinations.
The study reports annual growth of 14.7% in owned dog numbers.
More than 78% of adult female dogs were reported sterilized.
Questionnaire responses indicated higher lifetime receipt of at least one anti-rabies vaccination inside the municipality than outside it.
Questionnaire-reported annual vaccination coverage was 74.2% inside and 68.9% outside the municipality.
Household analyses attributed most observed variation in vaccination and sterilization coverage to geographic location rather than household dog count.
The systematic review included eight vaccination-only studies and eight studies of combined vaccination and sterilization.

hypotheses: Conversion from unsterilized to sterilized status could reduce the number requiring surgery without reducing total abundance.
Changes in survey effort, catchability, roaming behavior, or classification could change observed counts independently of abundance.
Births, abandonment, immigration, and emigration could affect counts within program boundaries and offset or resemble demographic effects of sterilization.
Repeated total-population surveys, individual identification, detection estimates, and consistent geographic and ownership definitions could help distinguish these explanations.

proposition_sample.statement: The Anuradhapura study assessed a five-year zoned CNVR program incorporating owner engagement and a peripheral buffer zone.
Sexually intact free-roaming dogs were captured along predefined routes with standardized effort during 2021–2025.
Owned dogs were voluntarily presented to program clinics.
The reported number of free-roaming dogs requiring sterilization declined from 1,368 in 2021 to 484 in 2025.
Annual declines in community dog counts per unit effort were not statistically significant.
The abstract reports significant buffer-intervention effects on male populations in zone 1.
The abstract reports significant buffer-intervention effects on female populations in zone 3.
Owned dog numbers were reported to increase by 14.7% annually.
Female dog ownership was reported to increase by 24.1%.
More than 78% of adult female dogs were reported sterilized.
Questionnaire responses indicated that 94.2% of owned dogs within the municipality had received at least one anti-rabies vaccination.
Questionnaire responses indicated that 83.1% of owned dogs outside the municipality had received at least one anti-rabies vaccination.
